learningObjective: Explain why shifting query and key positions by the same amount changes their absolute RoPE angles but leaves their relative attention contribution unchanged.
mediumRationale: A compact deterministic SVG is the smallest medium that can preserve exact vector angles and make the common-rotation cancellation directly inspectable at phone width.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected because a flowchart can locate RoPE before the attention dot product but cannot accurately preserve angular separation.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected because fixed vector geometry can show two absolute position pairs with the same offset and the same angle gap in one responsive figure.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected because a table can compare positions and formulas but still asks the reader to imagine the rotation geometry.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected because dragging token positions adds controls and state before the invariant itself is understood; two fixed examples prove the intended point.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected because the RoFormer paper's CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license does not permit adapted figure reuse, and its figures are denser than this single-invariant lesson. No source figure, coordinates, data, prose, or layout is copied.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected because the prose supplies the matrix identity but leaves the hardest mental step—how two absolute rotations cancel to a relative angle—for the reader to construct.

pages.insight: The transformer overview says decoder inputs are augmented with positional information, but it does not identify or explain rotary encoding.
The neighboring BERT and RoBERTa slide discusses masking, segments, and fixed 512-token training sequences without showing positional geometry.
The transformer-family summary covers attention scaling, normalization, residuals, and architecture variants but contains no RoPE mechanism.
The slide immediately before the direct match covers LLM data and scaling laws and provides no positional-encoding content.
The only direct RoPE match says OLMo replaces absolute positional embeddings with RoPE following LLaMA and PaLM; it names the choice but does not explain rotations or relative offsets.
The following compute-optimization slide writes the QK-transpose attention equation and discusses long-sequence cost, but it does not show where or how RoPE changes Q and K.
The sequence-packing slide says position IDs must reset at example boundaries, confirming that position semantics matter operationally without explaining rotary encoding.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is why position-dependent absolute rotations yield a relative attention score. For one 2D pair, orthogonal rotation gives (R_m q)^T(R_n k) = q^T R_m^T R_n k = q^T R_(n-m) k. The original schematic compares positions (1, 3) and their common shift (4, 6): both have n-m = 2 and therefore a 2-theta angular gap. It also makes the Q/K-only boundary explicit. Source review prompted two tightly related correctness clarifications in the article: a single frequency contribution oscillates rather than monotonically decays, and RoPE's defined formula beyond training length does not guarantee reliable extrapolation.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages, inspected both relevant slide neighborhoods, verified three primary papers and their arXiv license links, corrected two mechanism-adjacent overstatements, and reviewed the original geometry against the rotation identity.

implementation.accessibility: The SVG has a linked title and detailed description that state both position pairs, their equal offset, the preserved angle gap, the cancellation identity, and that values are unchanged. Query and key use both direct labels and solid-versus-dashed line styles, so color is not required. All conclusions and operations are written in text. The 360-unit viewBox has no minimum width and uses the established 11-pixel SVG label primitives for readability at 390 CSS pixels. Existing theme variables provide light/dark contrast; shared print rules force a light high-contrast palette and avoid splitting the figure.
